title: Density-Selected Topological Pathways in the Melting of Single-Particle-Thick Stripes
abstract: The melting of stripe-forming systems involves changes in connectivity that are not fully captured by conventional structural and orientational descriptors. We investigate a two-dimensional model with competing interactions whose low-temperature phase consists of one-particle-thick stripes. Molecular dynamics simulations along seven heating isochores are analyzed using thermodynamic, orientational, dynamical, and graph-based observables. Heating produces a multistage reconstruction in which the loss of stripe alignment and the reorganization of filament connectivity occur over distinct temperature ranges. Density controls whether the disordered filaments fragment into finite polymer-like clusters or remain joined in a dynamically fluid, system-spanning network. The topological observables distinguish these outcomes, which are not resolved by the thermodynamic and orientational responses alone. Thus, the same ordered stripe microphase can melt into topologically distinct fluids selected by density.
summary: This work simulates the melting of stripe phases in a 2D system, finding that density dictates the final fluid topology. The authors demonstrate that simple thermodynamic measurements fail to capture this complexity; only advanced topological observables can distinguish between a fragmented cluster state and a continuous network state.
main_problem: The study investigates how the melting of stripe-forming systems changes connectivity, specifically determining if the resulting fluid topology is uniquely determined by the initial ordered state or if it is instead selected by the system's density.
main_result: The topological outcome of the melt—whether the filaments fragment into finite clusters or remain in a dynamically fluid, system-spanning network—is strongly dependent on the particle density ($ho$).
method: Molecular dynamics simulations are performed along isochoric heating paths using various structural, orientational, and advanced graph-based topological observables.
model_or_system: The model is a two-dimensional system of particles interacting via a Lennard-Jones plus Gaussian (LJG) pair potential, which stabilizes one-particle-thick stripe phases at low temperatures.
key_observables: Topological descriptors like the first Betti number ($ eta_1$), graph 2-core fraction ($f_{2-	ext{core}}$), and connectivity measures are crucial alongside standard thermodynamic quantities like isochoric heat capacity ($c_V$).
important_parameters: The analysis spans seven densities ($ho = 0.395$ to $0.455$) across the stripe-forming regime, as well as varying temperatures during heating.
main_assumptions: Conventional scalar order parameters are insufficient because they cannot distinguish between a system-spanning network and finite clusters when local packing is similar; thus, topological diagnostics are necessary.
figures_summary: Figures summarize the density dependence of structural metrics (like nematic order $S_2$) during melting, showing that while global order decays uniformly, the topological structure diverges based on $ho$.
paper_structure: The paper analyzes the multistage reconstruction upon heating, contrasting the behavior observed using only thermodynamic/orientational data versus the richer information provided by graph-based topology to distinguish between different fluid states.
why_interesting: While focused on classical soft matter physics, the reliance on topological invariants (like Betti numbers) to characterize phase transitions and connectivity changes mirrors concepts used in analyzing complex quantum many-body ground states or entanglement structures.
